summaries.gardner: Sandisk has some Rule Breaker traits: spectacular momentum (up roughly 530% in 2026), a well-known consumer brand and a ride on the AI storage boom. But it is a fifth-ranked supplier in a mature, cyclical commodity industry rather than the top dog of an emerging one, and it lacks a visionary founder, so it fits Gardner's approach only partly.
summaries.buffett: Buffett looks for durable moats, consistent earnings and predictable cash flows, and Sandisk lost money in FY2023-FY2025 before earning $11,433M in FY2026 on a memory shortage. Its debt-free balance sheet and buybacks are positives, but NAND's commodity pricing and capital intensity make long-term earnings hard to predict, so it fits poorly.
summaries.munger: Munger favoured great businesses with lasting advantages and would invert the problem: NAND history is full of gluts that wiped out profits, and Sandisk's FY2026 gross margin of 71.5% is unlikely to persist. Its brand and Kioxia joint-venture scale are real, but this is the kind of cyclical, hard-to-predict business he usually avoided.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Sandisk as a cyclical, where a low P/E (about 6.5 times forward earnings) often signals a peak rather than a bargain. The story is simple—flash prices up on AI demand—but the key question is where the cycle stands, and insiders have been selling rather than buying.
summaries.fisher: Fisher prized long-term sales growth, strong R&D and management depth; Sandisk spends $1,328M a year on R&D and keeps launching new flash generations and products like UltraQLC and High Bandwidth Flash. But sales have swung sharply with the cycle, margins are not consistently superior, and the company has only been independent since 2025, so it partly fits.
summaries.graham: Graham's defensive criteria require ten years of profits, a long dividend record and moderate P/E and P/B, and Sandisk fails most: it lost money in FY2023-FY2025, pays no dividend, and trades at about 73 times three-year average earnings and 13 times book. Its strong current ratio and zero debt are the only clear passes.
summaries.thiel: Thiel looks for monopolies with technology ten times better than rivals, and Sandisk is one of five comparable NAND producers with no such lead. Its timing on AI storage is good and its distribution is strong, but it competes in a crowded, commoditised market, the opposite of his ideal.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on AI beneficiaries with improving fundamentals at sensible prices, and Sandisk's revenue nearly tripled to $20,248M in FY2026 with a forward P/E near 6.5 and $14B of new buyback authorisation. The question for him would be how long the shortage lasts and whether the cycle has peaked.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller's style of buying accelerating earnings with rising estimates and riding liquidity fits Sandisk's 2026 surge: EPS estimates for FY2027 rose from $208 to $215 over 90 days and the company beat estimates four quarters running. He would also watch closely for the turn in memory pricing, as the October 2026 selloff on Chinese capacity news showed.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants consistently high returns on capital, resilient pricing and low cyclicality, and Sandisk is a capital-intensive, cyclical hardware company with losses in three of the last four years before FY2026. It does not fit his 'good companies' test, though its current returns are exceptional.
summaries.greenblatt: On Greenblatt's Magic Formula Sandisk screens well right now: operating income of $12,389M is about 6.2% of its roughly $200B enterprise value, and return on capital is very high. But the formula uses trailing peak-cycle earnings, which can mislead for a memory maker.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high rates; Sandisk has competent management and a strong balance sheet, but its business is cyclical and its returns depend on industry pricing, so it fits only weakly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary distress bought with a big margin of safety; Sandisk was exactly that during the 2023-2025 glut, but at $1,403 after a roughly 600% one-year rise the stock prices in a strong cycle, so the 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup is not there now.
summaries.wood: Cathie Wood targets disruptive platforms with steeply falling costs; flash storage is an enabler of AI and its cost per bit keeps falling, but Sandisk is an incumbent component supplier rather than a disruptive platform leader, so it fits only partly.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and pricing power; Sandisk generated $11,494M of free cash flow in FY2026 and has no debt, but its earnings are highly unpredictable and its market position is not dominant.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for 'scale economics shared' businesses that pass savings to customers and grow stronger for decades; Sandisk's cost reductions are matched by rivals and its pricing follows the industry cycle, so it is far from his model.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products solving big problems; Sandisk's market (NAND, roughly $79B of supplier revenue in 2Q26 alone) is large and growing with AI, but it is an established spin-off rather than a new company creating a market.
summaries.nash: Sandisk scores well on Nash's numbers today—debt-free with $4,762M cash, 175% revenue growth, a 61% operating margin and four straight earnings beats—and it sells into the AI infrastructure trend. But it lacks a ten-year history as an independent company, its five-year record is volatile, insiders are selling, and his DCF does not support the price, so it is a partial fit.

momentum.evidence: The stock rose from about $199 in October 2025 to $1,403.34 on October 14, 2026 (roughly +600% in a year, about +530% in 2026), far ahead of the S&P 500, despite a pullback from its $2,354 high.

g4.evidence: CEO David Goeckeler, ex-Cisco and Western Digital CEO, executed the spin-off well, and it partners with Kioxia and SK hynix, but it has no famous anchor investor.

g6.evidence: Commentators debate whether its 84.6% Q4 FY2026 gross margin is sustainable and question a bubble after a ~600% rise, but on a forward P/E of about 6.5 many analysts call it cheap (consensus target $2,173).

simple.evidence: Making and selling flash memory is easy to describe, but forecasting NAND supply, pricing and the Kioxia joint-venture economics is hard for a generalist.

b2.evidence: Operating income swung from $1,200M (FY2022) to losses of $2,035M, $468M and $1,377M (FY2023-FY2025) and then $12,389M (FY2026).

integrity.evidence: Management repaid all $1,900M of debt and bought back $4,524M of stock in FY2026 with clear disclosures, but insiders sold about $121M of stock in the three months to October 2026 and there is a combined Chairman/CEO role.

b6.evidence: It stayed focused on flash after the spin-off rather than diversifying, though the March 2026 equity investment in DRAM maker Nanya shows some willingness to expand.

roic.evidence: FY2026 operating income of $12,389M on $15,736M of equity with no debt is an exceptional return, but returns were negative in FY2023-FY2025, so they are not consistent.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $11,494M ($11,671M operating cash flow minus $177M capex), about 100% of $11,433M net income, though FY2024-FY2025 free cash flow was negative.

b10.evidence: As an independent company only since February 2025, there is too little history to judge whether retained earnings created matching value.

safety.evidence: At $1,403 the stock trades at about 13 times book and 73 times its three-year average EPS, and a conservative through-cycle valuation is well below the price.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 6.5 on FY2027 EPS of $214.82 looks cheap, but those are peak-cycle earnings that may not last.

mu5.evidence: It can be hurt in many ways: a NAND glut, Chinese capacity (YMTC, CXMT), losing share, dependence on Kioxia's fabs, and weak PC/phone demand.

reinvest.evidence: AI storage demand gives room to reinvest via the Kioxia joint venture, but returns on new NAND capacity depend on industry pricing and fall in gluts.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic Lynch cyclical: profits surge when flash prices rise (FY2026 net income $11,433M) and vanish in gluts (FY2025 net loss $1,641M).

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 19 and forward P/E of about 6.5 are far below the 203% expected FY2027 EPS growth, though for a cyclical that is a classic peak warning.

runway.evidence: AI data-center storage and High Bandwidth Flash give years of demand, but revenue already nearly tripled at peak prices and will follow the cycle.

ly7.evidence: It bought back $4,524M of stock in FY2026 and outstanding shares are 146.4M, but insiders bought $0 and sold about $121M in the three months to October 2026, and diluted shares rose from 145M to 155M.

ly8.evidence: It is one of the most-watched AI memory stocks, covered by about 25 analysts with heavy media attention.

fi2.evidence: It keeps moving to new flash generations (BiCS8 218-layer) and new products such as 256TB UltraQLC SSDs and High Bandwidth Flash with SK hynix.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $1,328M in FY2026 delivered competitive flash generations and new SSD lines, but TrendForce still ranks it fifth in NAND revenue.

fi4.evidence: Its retail brand and distribution are strong in consumer storage, but it lags Samsung and SK hynix/Solidigm in enterprise SSD sales.

longterm.evidence: It keeps spending on R&D and next-generation technology like HBF, but in the 2026 boom it chose to keep bit shipment growth conservative and spend heavily on buybacks.

gr1.evidence: Market value is about $205B, FY2026 revenue was $20,248M and it has about 11,100 employees.

ni10.evidence: It posted net losses of $2,143M (FY2023), $672M (FY2024) and $1,641M (FY2025).

eps10.evidence: It has reported EPS only since its 2025 spin-off, so there is no ten-year record.

gr6.evidence: Three-year average diluted EPS is about $19.27 (-$4.63, -$11.32, $73.76), so $1,403 is about 73 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 19 times P/B of about 13 is roughly 250, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its BiCS flash is comparable to Samsung's, SK hynix's, Micron's and YMTC's, not ten times better.

timing.evidence: AI servers are driving an enterprise SSD shortage, and BMO expects NAND to stay undersupplied through 2027 and possibly 2028.

th3.evidence: It is a long-established player in a large NAND market, not a company that started with a big share of a small niche.

team.evidence: Goeckeler's management is experienced and executed the spin-off and debt paydown well, but it is not a world-class founder-led team.

th5.evidence: It sells through OEM relationships, hyperscaler qualifications and broad retail distribution of SanDisk-brand products worldwide.

durable.evidence: Flash will remain essential for 10-20 years and Sandisk has scale with Kioxia, but its share fell from about 14% (WD flash, 4Q20) to about 11% (2Q26) and Chinese rivals are rising.

th7.evidence: AI storage demand is visible to every memory maker; Sandisk's bets like High Bandwidth Flash are being pursued jointly with SK hynix.

trend.evidence: Datacenter revenue jumped from $960M in FY2025 to $5,153M in FY2026 as AI servers drove enterprise SSD demand.

dr1.evidence: Quarterly revenue rose to $8,965M in Q4 FY2026 with guidance of $10.3B-$10.8B for Q1 FY2027, and FY2027 EPS estimates rose from $208.22 to $214.82 over 90 days.

dr2.evidence: Whether it looks better in 18-24 months depends on NAND pricing, which analysts expect to stay tight into 2027 but which Chinese capacity and weaker devices demand could loosen.

dr4.evidence: AI capital spending is strong, but higher memory prices are hurting smartphone and PC demand, and the stock is sensitive to risk appetite for AI chips.

dr6.evidence: Q1 FY2027 results on October 29, 2026, the new $14B buyback authorisation and contract price increases are near-term catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Extreme cyclicality and volatility (the stock fell from $2,354 to about $1,403) make it unsuitable for a large concentrated position for most investors.

gm.evidence: FY2026 gross margin was 71.5% (84.6% in Q4), but it was 30.1% in FY2025 and about 7% in FY2023, so high margins reflect the cycle more than lasting pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $11,494M is about 5.6% of its roughly $205B market value, and much higher on FY2027 estimates.

gb2.evidence: FY2026 operating income of $12,389M is about 6.2% of an enterprise value of about $200B, a decent but peak-cycle earnings yield.

pa2.evidence: The industry is in a boom, not a setback; the recent temporary setback was the 2023-2025 glut.

pa4.evidence: With no debt and $4,762M cash the business is safe, but buying at a peak-cycle price after a ~600% rise risks large permanent capital loss if margins revert.

wo1.evidence: It is a significant supplier of storage for AI servers, but a component maker rather than an AI leader.

wo2.evidence: Flash cost per bit keeps falling as layer counts rise (BiCS8 218 layers), enabling huge capacity SSDs, though prices rose sharply in 2026.

wo3.evidence: It is focused on one platform, flash storage.

wo4.evidence: NAND demand is growing fast with AI, but the addressable market is unlikely to be many times larger in five years after the 2026 price surge.

ac3.evidence: Its results swing with memory chip prices, which are effectively a commodity, and with global device demand.

ns1.evidence: It raised prices sharply during the 2026 shortage rather than passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Its position in 10-20 years depends on NAND technology races and Chinese competition and is not clearly stronger than today.

va2.evidence: AI and cloud computing need vast, fast, low-power storage, and enterprise SSD shortages in 2026 show it is a painful bottleneck.

tn1.evidence: It sells infrastructure-layer storage into the AI trend (Datacenter revenue $5,153M in FY2026), but it is a decades-old flash business retrofitted to AI rather than built for it.

tn2.evidence: The market still often sees it as a memory-card maker, while Datacenter has become a fast-growing 25% of revenue (33% in Q4 FY2026).

tn3.evidence: It is a large cap and not Chinese or a startup, but memory chips behave much like a commodity producer.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew in FY2024-FY2026 ($6,663M, $7,355M, $20,248M), it earned $11,433M in FY2026, and it has $4,762M cash and no debt.

tn5.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was positive ($11,494M) and Q4 FY2026 FCF was $7,083M, but cash ($1,481M) did not exceed debt ($1,849M) at June 2025, and the term loan was only fully repaid during FY2026.

tn6.evidence: FY2026 revenue grew 175% to $20,248M and Q1 FY2027 guidance implies more than quadruple year-ago revenue.

tn7.evidence: FY2026 revenue growth of 175% plus an FCF margin of 56.8% far exceeds 40.

tn8.evidence: Revenue rose 175% in FY2026 while total operating expenses fell from $3,589M to $2,083M (R&D plus SG&A up 17.5%).

tn9.evidence: It passes on size, cash vs debt (no debt), short interest (3.3%), operating margin (61%), growth and earnings (four beats), but Sandisk has existed as an independent company only since 2025 (the original SanDisk was founded in 1988).

tn10.evidence: No major legal threat is known, but US-China export controls and trade policy affect memory makers and its China sales.

tn11.evidence: Sandisk provides flash memory and SSDs that help device makers, data centres and consumers store data quickly and cheaply, charging per unit sold; buyers pick it for capacity, price, qualification and the trusted SanDisk brand.

tn13.evidence: Total 95/130: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 10, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 5 (not verified), revenue vs expenses 10, return vs S&P 10 (since 2025 listing), moat 5, CEO 5, recession-proof pricing power 0, secular trend 10, culture/mission 5, talent 5, meeting the 75 threshold.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell 38% in FY2023, operating margin swung to losses in FY2023-FY2025, free cash flow was negative in FY2024-FY2025, and debt exceeded cash at June 2025.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 170x ($12,389M / $73M), assets excluding goodwill of $17,513M are 2.6x liabilities of $6,771M, current ratio is 2.3, and liabilities are 0.43x equity.

tn18.evidence: Goeckeler has strong recent execution but has been Sandisk CEO only since 2025, is not a founder, and has not made open-market purchases.

tn20.evidence: It beat consensus EPS in each of the last four quarters (e.g. $39.25 vs $34.51 in the June 2026 quarter).

tn21.evidence: No fraud or auditor concerns, but executives including the CTO sold shares near highs (about $121M in three months) and a $1.83B goodwill impairment was taken in FY2025.

tn22.evidence: It has $20,248M of revenue, strong profits and is buying back rather than issuing stock.

tn24.evidence: At a forward P/E of about 6.5 the price implies earnings falling back from FY2027 estimates, below current delivery, but that reflects expected cyclical normalisation.

tn25.evidence: Using a 3-year average FCF margin of about 16% and trimmed 25% growth, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth gives roughly $650 per share, below the $1,403 price.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 6.5 on FY2027 EPS growth of about 203% gives a PEG far below 1, though peak-cycle earnings make the multiple less reliable.
